reasons.reproducibility: Whole-bay restoration of 3.2 M adult clams across 64 plots of ~1,850 m2 in Shinnecock Bay needs permits and a restoration program.
reasons.effectiveness: Brown tide fell from 0.3-1.9x10^6 to <10^4 cells/mL and filtration time from ~3 months to 10 days, a large drop but correlational with no concurrent control.
reasons.cost: Buying and planting 3.2 million adult clams costs far over $5,000.
reasons.time: Effects emerged over 2012-2019 with surveys to 2021, i.e. years.
reasons.environment: Only native clams added; clams rose 18x, harvests 16x and chl a fell, with no non-target harm reported.

reasons.reproducibility: 300 L mesocosms of Peconic Bay water with live clams need a sponsor with tank space and a cell counter.
reasons.effectiveness: High-clam tanks held Aureococcus ~100x lower than no-clam tanks (>600,000 cells/mL), a large controlled effect.
reasons.cost: A few hundred litres of tank plus a few dozen hard clams is roughly $150-500.
reasons.time: Differences appeared within the 8-9 day run; clearing ~40% of volume per day acts within days.
reasons.environment: Only native clams added and retrievable; no rise in total biomass or species shift reported.

reasons.reproducibility: Mesocosms with eelgrass and three bivalve species need outdoor tanks and sourced seagrass, doable with a sponsor.
reasons.effectiveness: Chl a significantly lower with bivalves (p<0.05) but no magnitude reported and not HAB-specific.
reasons.cost: Tanks, eelgrass and bivalves at realistic densities likely $150-500.
reasons.time: Duration not reported; eelgrass growth endpoints imply weeks to months, scored conservatively.
reasons.environment: Native bivalves only; light and eelgrass growth rose (+48%); no harm reported.

reasons.reproducibility: 13 m3 MERL mesocosms at Narragansett Bay are specialized facilities a school cannot reproduce.
reasons.effectiveness: Measured +58% sedimentation, not an algal reduction; shows lab rates overestimate field removal by up to 10x.
reasons.cost: Large mesocosm facility operation exceeds $5,000.
reasons.time: Duration not reported; sedimentation budgets of this kind run weeks to months, scored conservatively.
reasons.environment: Native clams only, but 21% of extra sediment became permanent biodeposits; no harm reported.

reasons.reproducibility: Lab particle-retention measurement with bivalves and a particle counter is a standard bench method, doable at school with a sponsor.
reasons.effectiveness: Clams retain 100% of particles >4 um and oysters 100% >5-6 um, but no bloom reduction measured and abstract digits partly unreadable.
reasons.cost: Six bivalve species plus tanks roughly $50-150 if a particle counter is borrowed.
reasons.time: Filtration rates are measured in hours.
reasons.environment: Nothing added to natural water; not reported otherwise.

reasons.reproducibility: Lab flow-through feeding with three common bivalves is a bench protocol a sponsor could supervise.
reasons.effectiveness: Ranks feeding clam < oyster < mussel with clam removal falling at high food; no HAB reduction measured.
reasons.cost: Bivalves, pumps and algal food roughly $50-150.
reasons.time: Feeding and biodeposition measured over hours.
reasons.environment: Nothing added; not reported, but a lab feeding study has no release.

reasons.reproducibility: Meta-analysis of >60 studies; the typical experiment is lab/field clearance measurement needing specialist gear.
reasons.effectiveness: Most studies deplete <30% of particles, a weak removal effect.
reasons.cost: Typical clearance-rate study with animals and counters ~$150-500.
reasons.time: Summarized aquaculture-biofilter effects are seasonal; review scored at weeks to months.
reasons.environment: Filter feeders add nothing; no harm reported.

reasons.reproducibility: Method review; the typical clearance experiment (beaker, bivalve, cell counts, Coughlan formula) is doable with a sponsor.
reasons.effectiveness: No algal reduction reported; review of measurement methods only.
reasons.cost: A clearance-rate setup is ~$50-150.
reasons.time: Clearance runs take hours.
reasons.environment: Nothing added in clearance tests; not reported.

reasons.reproducibility: 250 mL beakers with one 10-20 mm clam and cell counts over 1 h is a simple school bench protocol (culture purchase aside).
reasons.effectiveness: Clams cleared Margalefidinium at <=1,000 cells/mL but clearance was ~0 at >=1,500 cells/mL, i.e. fails at bloom densities.
reasons.cost: Small seed clams and beakers are under $50 beyond the cultures.
reasons.time: Result visible in 1 h.
reasons.environment: Clams only; no change in valve behaviour, nothing added.

reasons.reproducibility: Five bivalve species and toxic Alexandrium, Prorocentrum and Heterosigma cultures need a sponsor.
reasons.effectiveness: Bivalves cleared HAB cells as fast as or faster than Rhodomonas, but many cells came out intact and possibly viable in biodeposits and oysters stayed mostly closed.
reasons.cost: Bivalves and three HAB cultures cost $150-500.
reasons.time: 1 h clearance incubations.
reasons.environment: Viable HAB cells and Alexandrium temporary cysts were repackaged in feces and pseudofeces.

reasons.reproducibility: The 1 L beaker clearance test is simple, but it needs Dinophysis bloom water, field deployments and toxin LC-MS.
reasons.effectiveness: Measures clearance rates (oysters 1.69 L/h/g) only, not any reduction of the bloom.
reasons.cost: Toxin analysis and deployments cost $500-5,000.
reasons.time: Clearance was measured in 60 min trials.
reasons.environment: Blue mussels exceeded the FDA DST guideline for three weeks and toxins persisted ~6 weeks.

reasons.reproducibility: Monitors a commercial oyster FLUPSY in an estuary.
reasons.effectiveness: Median chlorophyll removal across the nursery was 6.45%, sometimes negative, and too small to affect the embayment.
reasons.cost: A commercial FLUPSY costs well over $5,000.
reasons.time: Data spanned a four-month season.
reasons.environment: Oysters released biodeposits (negative removal) and died more during a Cochlodinium bloom.

reasons.reproducibility: Observation of the 1985 Narragansett Bay brown tide cannot be repeated on demand.
reasons.effectiveness: Negative: clearance fell above 5x10^5 cells/mL, so mussels did not control the ~10^6 cells/mL bloom.
reasons.cost: Bay-wide field survey far exceeds $5,000.
reasons.time: Over the course of a season-long bloom.
reasons.environment: 30-100% mussel mortality and complete reproductive failure.

reasons.reproducibility: Lab mussel feeding with a toxic Alexandrium culture needs purchased toxic cultures and toxin assays.
reasons.effectiveness: Clearance on Alexandrium ~48% lower than on the diatom; grazing weakened on the HAB.
reasons.cost: Toxic cultures and PST analysis ~$150-500 excluding assay lab.
reasons.time: Ran 17 d; toxicity passed the limit in <1 h, but the removal question spans weeks.
reasons.environment: Mussels kept 79% of ingested toxin and became unsafe to eat; no mortality.

reasons.reproducibility: Lab clams fed two Alexandrium isolates need toxic cultures and toxin analysis.
reasons.effectiveness: Clams ate the high-toxicity strain only when diatom was added; little removal of the HAB itself.
reasons.cost: Cultures, clams and toxin testing ~$150-500.
reasons.time: ~2 weeks uptake.
reasons.environment: Tissues exceeded closure level by several orders of magnitude, with 3-6 week depuration.

reasons.reproducibility: Oyster life stages with a Prorocentrum culture plus histology needs sponsor lab access.
reasons.effectiveness: Juveniles rejected most P. minimum as pseudofeces for ~2 weeks; little effective removal.
reasons.cost: Oyster seed, cultures and histology ~$150-500.
reasons.time: Effects over weeks.
reasons.environment: Larvae grew poorly on P. minimum, a minor non-target effect on the oysters.

reasons.reproducibility: Oysters, Asian clams and a toxic Microcystis culture in 1 L beakers need a sponsor and toxin assays.
reasons.effectiveness: Clams cleared cultured Microcystis but in bloom water both bivalves cleared slowly and clams selected green algae over cyanobacteria.
reasons.cost: Bivalves, culture and microcystin assays cost $150-500.
reasons.time: Toxin accumulation was measurable at 24 h in 3-4 day trials.
reasons.environment: Oysters accumulated up to 4905 ng/g microcystin, orders of magnitude over guidance, without depurating.

reasons.reproducibility: Upstream-downstream fluorometry over eight intertidal oyster reefs is field work.
reasons.effectiveness: Reefs removed a mean of 12.9% of chlorophyll, ranging from -9.8% to 27.9%, with one short run per reef.
reasons.cost: Field fluorometers and reef access cost over $5,000.
reasons.time: Measurement runs lasted 0.3-1.3 h.
reasons.environment: Natural reefs add nothing and bare shell removed no chlorophyll.

reasons.reproducibility: Model study; running a published eutrophication model is possible on a computer, though this Chesapeake model is specialist.
reasons.effectiveness: Even 10x oyster biomass cut summer surface chl by only ~1 mg/m3.
reasons.cost: Model runs cost nothing beyond a computer.
reasons.time: Effect is a summer-season outcome of multi-year restoration.
reasons.environment: Oysters add nothing; deep DO +0.25 g/m3 and SAV +20%.

reasons.reproducibility: Seasonal flux measurements on a restored reef in the Choptank River need field cores and nutrient analysis.
reasons.effectiveness: Measured nutrient fluxes, not algae; no algal reduction reported.
reasons.cost: Reef restoration and flux campaign exceed $5,000.
reasons.time: All seasons measured.
reasons.environment: Ammonium and phosphate release >=10x control, which can fuel algae.

reasons.reproducibility: Running the FARM and EcoWin ecosystem models requires specialist modelling software and data.
reasons.effectiveness: Modelled chlorophyll fell only 1.3-2.1% on average (0.3% farm-scale).
reasons.cost: A modelling study can be repeated with free or web tools.
reasons.time: Model outcomes are annual.
reasons.environment: Oyster aquaculture removes nitrogen with no added material.

reasons.reproducibility: Theoretical model comparing recycling and growth timescales is reproducible with a spreadsheet.
reasons.effectiveness: Theory only: gives conditions for control, no measured algal reduction.
reasons.cost: Free to repeat.
reasons.time: No experimental time; the control acts over ecosystem timescales, scored conservatively.
reasons.environment: Natural benthos, nothing added; not reported.

reasons.reproducibility: Bivalves in 5 L microcosms with a Thalassiosira culture and counting chamber are simple.
reasons.effectiveness: Removal was 77-94% in triplicate, but with no bivalve-free control, settling or die-off cannot be separated from filtration.
reasons.cost: Bivalves, culture and a counting chamber cost about $50-150.
reasons.time: 5 day experiment.
reasons.environment: Bivalves are retrievable and also cleared nutrients and wastewater solids.

reasons.reproducibility: Lab clearance with Rhodomonas plus yellow loess clay is bench-scale but uses seven invertebrate species.
reasons.effectiveness: Tests clay interference with filtration, not algal removal; scallop clearance fell at 0.01 g/L.
reasons.cost: Seven species, culture and loess ~$150-500.
reasons.time: Clearance measured in hours.
reasons.environment: Loess clay suppressed scallop and mussel clearance at 0.01-10 g/L, a non-target effect.
